title: Real, but not significant yet
summary: Averaged over the whole Tibetan Plateau, temperature is rising, but natural ups and downs are large. How many more years until we can be sure?

steps.message: Testing significance (Mann-Kendall and t-test, both corrected for autocorrelation)...

Mann-Kendall p = 0.1021 — the trend is not statistically significant at alpha=0.05. Sen's slope 95% CI: [-0.001879, 0.01992] per year. t-test p = 0.1750 with an effective sample size of 236 (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.29). Not significant yet: a trend this size typically needs about 57 years of data to be detected; this record has 36.

finding.title: Temperature at 2 Meters in Tibetan Plateau, 1990-2025
finding.statistical_method: Sen's slope with a Mann-Kendall test on monthly anomalies (seasonal cycle removed), both corrected for lag-1 autocorrelation (r1 = 0.29); OLS t-test with effective sample size n_eff = 236 as a second check
finding.importance_note: Effect size = |total change| / std. dev. = 0.82 — the observed change is large relative to natural year-to-year variability. A statistically significant trend can still have a small effect size; significance and scientific/practical importance are evaluated separately here.

finding.interpretation: The 2‑meter temperature over the Tibetan Plateau shows a modest positive trend of 0.092 °C per decade between 1990 and 2025, but the overall trend is not statistically significant (p = 0.102, 95 % CI –0.0019 to 0.0199 °C yr⁻¹). The autumn (SON) season exhibits a significant warming of 0.219 °C per decade (p = 0.028), whereas winter, spring, and summer trends are not significant. Spatial analysis reveals that roughly 48 % of grid cells show significant warming while about 3 % show significant cooling, indicating heterogeneous regional responses. The effect‑size note (0.82) suggests the observed change is large relative to natural inter‑annual variability, even though statistical significance is lacking.
finding.limitations: Statistical power is limited; the effective sample size of 236 and the estimated 57 years needed to detect the trend imply low confidence in the observed change. The overall trend is classified as not robust, and the significance assessment does not account for potential unmodeled confounding factors.

provenance.source_name: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
provenance.processing_method: Monthly NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) values on 336 grid cells averaged over the region with cos(latitude) area weights (a month counts only when at least 70% of the region's area has data), the average seasonal cycle (monthly climatology over the record) subtracted to give anomalies, then trend-tested; annual means are shown for reference.
provenance.statistical_method: Sen's slope with a Mann-Kendall test on monthly anomalies (seasonal cycle removed), both corrected for lag-1 autocorrelation (r1 = 0.29); OLS t-test with effective sample size n_eff = 236 as a second check

concern_reasons: The trend is not statistically clear, so no judgement is made.
confidence_reasons: The robustness check says the trend does not hold up across both halves of the record.

evidence.text: Parts of the region move in opposite directions (42 grid cells rising, 3 falling), so one regional story is too simple.
The underlying data is reanalysis (model-assimilated) averaged over the region's grid cells, so a trend can partly reflect changes in the observing system rather than the climate.
